issues.legal_issue: The service provider, rather than the recipient, is the person statutorily liable to pay service tax on a rental service unless the law assigns liability to another person.
material_facts: The dispute concerned service tax on the rental of commercial premises by a lessor to a government lessee.
The lease was made after the introduction of the charge on services under Section 66B of the Finance Act, 1994.
The service was provided by the lessor, and the applicable rules did not assign liability for this rental service to the recipient.
issues.conclusion: The lessor, as the provider of the rental service, was the person liable to pay the service tax; the tax’s indirect economic character did not make the lessee the statutory taxpayer.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 65(7), 66B and 68(1) of the Finance Act, 1994, read with Rule 2(1)(d) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994, identify the provider as the person liable in an ordinary case, subject to notified exceptions. Service tax may be passed on economically, but that does not determine who is legally assessed. Tamil Nadu Kalyana Mandapam Assn. v. Union of India; All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India; Association of Leasing & Financial Service Companies v. Union of India; Godfrey Phillips India Ltd. v. State of U.P.; Babu Ram Jagdish Kumar & Co. v. State of Punjab; Chhotabhai Jethabhai Patel & Co. v. Union of India; The matter of the Central Provinces and Berar Sales of Motor Spirit and Lubricants Taxation Act, 1938; and R.C. Jall v. Union of India support the distinction between the taxable event, the person liable, and the economic incidence of a tax. Section 12B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, applied to service tax through Section 83 of the Finance Act, concerns the burden of proving that tax was not passed on when seeking a refund; it does not determine the person primarily liable.

predicates.service_tax_rental_dispute: The proceeding concerns who is legally liable to pay service tax on a rental service.
predicates.provider_supplies_rental_service: A person other than the recipient provides the rental service.
predicates.recipient_is_not_designated_payer: The applicable law does not assign payment liability for the service to the recipient.

issues.definition: When a service-tax dispute concerns a rental service supplied by one person to another and the recipient is not designated as payer, the provider is statutorily liable.

issues.legal_issue: A lease clause allocating taxes primarily leviable on the lessor to the lessor places the contractual burden of rental-service tax on the lessor when the lessor is the person assessed for that tax.
material_facts: The lease required the lessor to pay taxes primarily leviable on the lessor and the government lessee to pay taxes primarily leviable on the occupier.
Under the applicable service-tax law and rules, the lessor providing the rental service was the person liable for the tax.
issues.conclusion: Under the law and the lease clause, the government lessee was not required to bear the service tax; the tax was primarily leviable on the lessor.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “primarily leviable upon” refers to the person legally liable for the tax, meaning the person on whom assessment is made, rather than the person who may ultimately bear the tax’s economic cost. “Levy” includes assessment but does not include collection: Peekay Re-Rolling Mills (P) Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner. The lessor was the assessed taxpayer under Sections 66B and 68 of the Finance Act, 1994, and Rule 2(1)(d) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994; the lease therefore allocated the tax to the lessor under its terms.

predicates.lease_tax_allocation_dispute: The parties dispute who bears a tax under a lease clause allocating taxes by reference to the person on whom they are primarily leviable.
predicates.service_provider_is_assessed_taxpayer: The person providing the service is the person legally assessed for the tax.
predicates.lease_allocates_primary_tax_to_lessor: The lease assigns taxes primarily leviable on the lessor to the lessor.

issues.definition: If a lease allocates taxes primarily leviable on the lessor to the lessor, and the service provider is the assessed taxpayer, the lessor bears the tax under the clause.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decline discretionary interference with a judgment requiring the recipient to bear service tax when the recipient expressly accepted that liability in written hiring communications and the judgment rested on those communications.
material_facts: A government sanction letter stated that service taxes, if applicable, were the lessee’s liability.
A later government letter to the lessor reiterated that allocation.
The single Judge relied on the later letter in finding that the government lessee was liable to bear the service tax.
Although the Supreme Court held that the lessee was not required to pay under the law and lease clause, it declined to disturb the result based on the government’s written communications.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the appellate judgment’s legal reasoning but refused discretionary relief under Article 136 of the Constitution; the appeal therefore failed on the facts.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 confers discretionary appellate jurisdiction. Although the statutory and lease-based legal position did not require the lessee to pay the tax, the Court declined to exercise its discretion in the lessee’s favour in light of the written communications expressly placing service-tax liability on it.

rule.if: constitutional_discretionary_appeal and written_hiring_terms_assign_service_tax_to_recipient and recipient_reaffirms_tax_commitment and lower_court_relies_on_commitment

predicates.constitutional_discretionary_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which the Supreme Court is asked to exercise discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.written_hiring_terms_assign_service_tax_: Written hiring terms state that the recipient is to bear applicable service tax.
predicates.recipient_reaffirms_tax_commitment: The recipient sends or adopts a further written communication affirming its responsibility for the tax.
predicates.lower_court_relies_on_commitment: The lower court relies on the recipient’s written commitment in deciding who must bear the tax.

issues.definition: When a recipient’s written hiring terms and further written commitment assign it the tax burden, and the lower court relies on that commitment, the Supreme Court may decline discretionary interference in the appeal.
